The Quartic Hessian Conjecture in Dimension Four

Zixiang Ni Email: akie.camellia@gmail.com
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The Hessian conjecture asks whether a polynomial with nonzero constant Hessian determinant has a polynomial gradient inverse. It is known in dimensions at most three, false in dimensions at least five, and open in dimension four. We prove its four-variable quartic case.

The top homogeneous part has zero Hessian determinant and, by the four-dimensional homogeneous Hesse theorem, is a cone. We divide its cone representative into three exhaustive types: a genuinely ternary quartic with nonzero ternary Hessian, a genuinely binary quartic, and a fourth power of a linear form. In the first type, the degree-seven determinant equation forces the cubic part to be affine-linear in the cone direction. In the binary type, the degree-six equation gives a constant null direction in a two-variable Hessian of the cubic part. In the unary type, the degree-five equation and a constant-direction lemma give the same conclusion. Every type therefore reduces to

f=P⁡(x1,x2,x3)+x4​Q​(x1,x2,x3)+a​x42,deg⁡Q≤2.f=P(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+x_{4}Q(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+ax_{4}^{2},\qquad\deg Q\leq 2.

We prove, independently of the degree or top part of PP, that every constant-Hessian polynomial of this form has a polynomial gradient inverse. The branch a≠0a\neq 0 descends from the known three-dimensional Hessian conjecture after a Schur complement. When a=0a=0, an isotropic-cone rank analysis eliminates rank two, solves the rank-one exception by an explicit triangular inverse, and reduces rank zero to the two-dimensional Hessian conjecture. The coupled degree-six identity is retained throughout; no component with respect to a fixed quadratic form is separated.

1 Introduction

For f∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], write

Hess⁡(f)=(∂i∂jf)i,j,∇f=(∂1f,…,∂nf).\operatorname{Hess}(f)=(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}f)_{i,j},\qquad\nabla f=(\partial_{1}f,\ldots,\partial_{n}f).
Definition 1.1 (Hessian conjecture, HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n}).

If detHess⁡(f)∈ℂ×\det\operatorname{Hess}(f)\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}, then ∇f:ℂn→ℂn\nabla f:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is a polynomial automorphism.

The conjecture is elementary for n=1n=1, was proved for n=2n=2 by Dillen [1], and was proved for n=3n=3 by de Bondt [2]. It is false for n≥5n\geq 5 [3], and is open only for n=4n=4. Moreover, HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4} implies the plane Jacobian conjecture by the standard doubling construction [4]. In degree at most two the gradient is affine, while a cubic potential has quadratic gradient and is covered by Wang’s theorem on quadratic Keller maps [5]. Thus degree four is the first unresolved degree in dimension four. A related boundary case was already known: Hubbers proved the Jacobian conjecture for cubic-homogeneous Keller maps in dimension four [6]. After normalizing the invertible linear part of the gradient, this covers potentials of the form f4+f2+f1+f0f_{4}+f_{2}+f_{1}+f_{0}, with fif_{i} homogeneous of degree ii: if A=Hess⁡(f2)A=\operatorname{Hess}(f_{2}), then constancy of the Hessian determinant gives detA≠0\det A\neq 0, and A−1​(∇f−∇f​(0))=x+H3​(x)A^{-1}(\nabla f-\nabla f(0))=x+H_{3}(x) with H3H_{3} cubic homogeneous. The result below allows an arbitrary cubic part as well, and hence treats every quartic potential.

Theorem 1.2 (Main theorem).

Let f∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4]f\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}] have degree four. If

detHess⁡(f)∈ℂ×,\det\operatorname{Hess}(f)\in\mathbb{C}^{\times},

then ∇f\nabla f is a polynomial automorphism of ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4}.

The proof has two logically separate parts. First, the top homogeneous form is classified and each possible type is shown to produce a constant direction in the cubic part. Second, a uniform proposition in that direction proves invertibility without any nondegeneracy assumption on the top form.

Remark 1.3 (The corrected degree-six equation).

In the genuinely ternary branch, write

f4=φ⁡(x1,x2,x3),f3=g⁡(x1,x2,x3)+x4​h​(x1,x2,x3),f_{4}=\varphi(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),\qquad f_{3}=g(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+x_{4}h(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),

and A=Hess3⁡(φ)A=\operatorname{Hess}_{3}(\varphi). If the x42x_{4}^{2}-coefficient of f2f_{2} is aa, the degree-six determinant equation is

2adetA−(∇h)𝖳adj(A)∇h=0.2a\det A-(\nabla h)^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{adj}(A)\nabla h=0.

The two terms may cancel: hh is a fixed polynomial, not a free parameter. The proof never separates them and does not attempt to deduce a=0a=0.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Coordinate changes and cone tops

All changes of variables below are constant invertible linear maps or source translations. If f~=f∘T\widetilde{f}=f\circ T, then

∇f~​(x)=T𝖳​(∇f)​(T​x),Hess⁡(f~)​(x)=T𝖳​Hess⁡(f)​(T​x)​T.\nabla\widetilde{f}(x)=T^{\mathsf{T}}(\nabla f)(Tx),\qquad\operatorname{Hess}(\widetilde{f})(x)=T^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{Hess}(f)(Tx)T.

Thus the Hessian determinant changes only by a nonzero constant factor and gradient invertibility is preserved. Source translations have the analogous affine-conjugacy property and do not alter the top homogeneous part.

Lemma 2.1 (Top homogeneous Hessian).

Let f=∑k=0dfkf=\sum_{k=0}^{d}f_{k} be the decomposition into homogeneous parts, with d≥3d\geq 3. If detHess⁡(f)\det\operatorname{Hess}(f) is constant, then

detHess⁡(fd)≡0.\det\operatorname{Hess}(f_{d})\equiv 0.
Proof.

The entries of Hess⁡(fk)\operatorname{Hess}(f_{k}) have degree k−2k-2. The homogeneous component of maximal possible degree n⁡(d−2)n(d-2) in the determinant is obtained by taking Hess⁡(fd)\operatorname{Hess}(f_{d}) in every entry, hence equals detHess⁡(fd)\det\operatorname{Hess}(f_{d}). A constant determinant has no positive-degree component. ∎

Theorem 2.2 (Homogeneous Hesse theorem in low dimension).

Let hh be homogeneous in 2≤n≤42\leq n\leq 4 variables over ℂ\mathbb{C}. If detHess⁡(h)=0\det\operatorname{Hess}(h)=0, then after a constant invertible linear change, hh depends on at most n−1n-1 variables.

Proof.

This is the low-dimensional case of the classical theorem of Gordan and Noether [7]; see de Bondt [8, Theorem 3.1] for a modern statement and proof in dimensions at most four. ∎

Lemma 2.3 (Binary forms with zero Hessian).

Let h∈ℂ⁡[X,Y]h\in\mathbb{C}[X,Y] be homogeneous of degree d≥2d\geq 2. Then

hX​XhY​Y−hX​Y2≡0⟺h=κLdh_{XX}h_{YY}-h_{XY}^{2}\equiv 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h=\kappa L^{d}

for some κ∈ℂ\kappa\in\mathbb{C} and linear form LL, with h=0h=0 allowed.

Proof.

On Y≠0Y\neq 0, write h⁡(X,Y)=Yd​p​(t)h(X,Y)=Y^{d}p(t), t=X/Yt=X/Y. Direct differentiation gives

detHess2⁡(h)=(d−1)​Y2​d−4​(d​p​p′′−(d−1)​(p′)2).\det\operatorname{Hess}_{2}(h)=(d-1)Y^{2d-4}\bigl(dpp^{\prime\prime}-(d-1)(p^{\prime})^{2}\bigr).

Suppose p≠0p\neq 0 and put q=p′/p∈ℂ⁡(t)q=p^{\prime}/p\in\mathbb{C}(t). Dividing the vanishing equation by p2p^{2} gives

d​q′+q2=0.dq^{\prime}+q^{2}=0.

If q=0q=0, then pp is constant. Otherwise (1/q)′=1/d(1/q)^{\prime}=1/d, so q=d/(t−α)q=d/(t-\alpha) for some α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}. Therefore

(p(t−α)d)′=0,\left(\frac{p}{(t-\alpha)^{d}}\right)^{\prime}=0,

and the constant field of ℂ⁡(t)\mathbb{C}(t) is ℂ\mathbb{C}. Thus p=κ​(t−α)dp=\kappa(t-\alpha)^{d}. Homogenization gives the assertion. The case p=0p=0 is immediate, as is the converse. ∎

2.2 Matrix identities and inverse descent

Lemma 2.4 (Block determinant).

For a square matrix BB and a column vector vv of the same size,

det(Bvv𝖳0)=−v𝖳​adj⁡(B)​v.\det\begin{pmatrix}B&v\\ v^{\mathsf{T}}&0\end{pmatrix}=-v^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{adj}(B)v.
Proof.

Expand along the last row and column, or use the polynomial continuation of the Schur-complement formula from invertible BB. ∎

Lemma 2.5 (Adjugate quadratic form).

For a symmetric 3×33\times 3 matrix MM and column vectors x,ℓx,\ell,

(M​x+ℓ)𝖳​adj⁡(M)​(M​x+ℓ)=det(M)​(x𝖳​M​x+2​ℓ𝖳​x)+ℓ𝖳​adj⁡(M)​ℓ.(Mx+\ell)^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{adj}(M)(Mx+\ell)=\det(M)\bigl(x^{\mathsf{T}}Mx+2\ell^{\mathsf{T}}x\bigr)+\ell^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{adj}(M)\ell.
Proof.

Expand by bilinearity and use M​adj⁡(M)=adj⁡(M)​M=det(M)​IM\operatorname{adj}(M)=\operatorname{adj}(M)M=\det(M)I, together with symmetry. ∎

Lemma 2.6 (Descent of a polynomial inverse).

Let R=ℂ⁡[t1,…,tm]R=\mathbb{C}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}], K=Frac⁡(R)K=\operatorname{Frac}(R), and F∈R​[x1,…,xn]nF\in R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]^{n}. Assume

detJx​F∈R×=ℂ×,F−1∈K​[y1,…,yn]n.\det J_{x}F\in R^{\times}=\mathbb{C}^{\times},\qquad F^{-1}\in K[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}]^{n}.

Then F−1∈R​[y1,…,yn]nF^{-1}\in R[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}]^{n}.

Proof.

Subtract F⁡(0)F(0) from the target and let L=Jx​F​(0)L=J_{x}F(0). Since detL∈ℂ×\det L\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}, an affine target change reduces to

F~​(x)=x+H⁡(x),H∈R​[x]n,ordx⁡H≥2.\widetilde{F}(x)=x+H(x),\qquad H\in R[x]^{n},\qquad\operatorname{ord}_{x}H\geq 2.

The unique formal inverse has the expansion

F~−1​(y)=y+∑d≥2Gd​(y),\widetilde{F}^{-1}(y)=y+\sum_{d\geq 2}G_{d}(y),

where GdG_{d} is homogeneous of yy-degree dd. Comparing total degree in F~​(F~−1​(y))=y\widetilde{F}(\widetilde{F}^{-1}(y))=y recursively expresses each GdG_{d} over RR. The inverse over KK is this same formal inverse and is a polynomial, so only finitely many GdG_{d} are nonzero. Undoing the affine target changes proves the claim. ∎

Lemma 2.7 (Transfer to characteristic-zero fields).

If HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} holds over ℂ\mathbb{C}, then it holds over every field of characteristic zero.

Proof.

Let KK have characteristic zero and let f∈K⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] have nonzero constant Hessian determinant. Choose a subfield k⊂Kk\subset K, finitely generated over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, which contains the coefficients of ff and the inverse of that determinant. Every finitely generated characteristic-zero field embeds in ℂ\mathbb{C}: choose a transcendence basis over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, send it to algebraically independent complex numbers, and extend across the resulting finite algebraic extension. After such an embedding, HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} over ℂ\mathbb{C} supplies a polynomial inverse of ∇f\nabla f.

To descend it, subtract ∇f​(0)\nabla f(0) from the target and normalize the invertible linear part. The coefficients of the unique formal inverse are then determined recursively from coefficients in kk, exactly as in Lemma 2.6; hence they lie in kk. The polynomial inverse over ℂ\mathbb{C} coincides with this formal inverse, so only finitely many of these coefficients are nonzero. It therefore belongs to k​[y]nk[y]^{n}, and hence gives an inverse over KK. ∎

3 Classification of quartic cone tops

Let f=f4+f3+f2+f1+f0f=f_{4}+f_{3}+f_{2}+f_{1}+f_{0} have degree four and nonzero constant Hessian determinant. Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 2.2 allow a linear change after which

f4=φ⁡(x1,x2,x3).f_{4}=\varphi(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}).

There are three exhaustive cases.

  1. 1.

    If detHess3⁡(φ)≢0\det\operatorname{Hess}_{3}(\varphi)\not\equiv 0, the top is genuinely ternary.

  2. 2.

    If detHess3⁡(φ)≡0\det\operatorname{Hess}_{3}(\varphi)\equiv 0, Theorem 2.2 in three variables makes φ\varphi binary. If its binary Hessian is nonzero, the top is genuinely binary.

  3. 3.

    If the binary Hessian also vanishes, Lemma 2.3 gives φ=c​L4\varphi=cL^{4}. Since ff has degree four, c≠0c\neq 0; after a linear change the top is unary, f4=c​x14f_{4}=cx_{1}^{4}.

The next two sections show that all three cases lead to the same structural form.

4 The genuinely ternary top

Assume

f4=φ⁡(x1,x2,x3),A=Hess3⁡(φ),detA≢0.f_{4}=\varphi(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),\qquad A=\operatorname{Hess}_{3}(\varphi),\qquad\det A\not\equiv 0.

Put

H4=Hess⁡(f4)=(A000),Hk=Hess⁡(fk).H_{4}=\operatorname{Hess}(f_{4})=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad H_{k}=\operatorname{Hess}(f_{k}).

4.1 The degree-seven equation

The degree-seven part of det(H4+H3+H2)\det(H_{4}+H_{3}+H_{2}) contains three entries of H4H_{4} and one of H3H_{3}. It is the first variation

tr⁡(adj⁡(H4)​H3).\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(H_{4})H_{3}\bigr).

The adjugate of H4H_{4} has only one possibly nonzero entry, namely (adj⁡H4)44=detA(\operatorname{adj}H_{4})_{44}=\det A. Therefore

0=detA​∂44f3.0=\det A\,\partial_{44}f_{3}.

The polynomial ring is a domain and detA≠0\det A\neq 0, so

f3=g⁡(x1,x2,x3)+x4​h​(x1,x2,x3),f_{3}=g(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+x_{4}h(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),

where gg is cubic and hh is quadratic.

4.2 The coupled degree-six equation

Write

f2=q⁡(x1,x2,x3)+x4​ℓ​(x1,x2,x3)+a​x42,f_{2}=q(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+x_{4}\ell(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+ax_{4}^{2},

where qq is quadratic, ℓ\ell is linear, and a∈ℂa\in\mathbb{C}. Degree six has exactly two types of contribution:

(2,2,2,0)and(2,2,1,1),(2,2,2,0)\quad\text{and}\quad(2,2,1,1),

where the numbers denote entry degrees. The first gives 2​a​detA2a\det A. In the second, the two H4H_{4}-entries exhaust the first three coordinates except for one row and column, while the last row and column come from Hess⁡(x4​h)\operatorname{Hess}(x_{4}h). The block expansion gives

−(∇h)𝖳adj(A)∇h.-(\nabla h)^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{adj}(A)\nabla h.

Thus

2adetA−(∇h)𝖳adj(A)∇h=0.2a\det A-(\nabla h)^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{adj}(A)\nabla h=0. (1)

No separation of its two fixed summands is made.

Combining the preceding forms and absorbing f1,f0f_{1},f_{0} gives the following.

Proposition 4.1 (Ternary structural reduction).

In the genuinely ternary case, after the cone-coordinate change,

f=P⁡(x1,x2,x3)+x4​Q​(x1,x2,x3)+a​x42,deg⁡Q≤2.f=P(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+x_{4}Q(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+ax_{4}^{2},\qquad\deg Q\leq 2.

5 The degenerate cone tops

5.1 The genuinely binary top

Assume

f4=φ⁡(x1,x2),A=Hess2⁡(φ),detA≢0.f_{4}=\varphi(x_{1},x_{2}),\qquad A=\operatorname{Hess}_{2}(\varphi),\qquad\det A\not\equiv 0.

Put X=(x1,x2)X=(x_{1},x_{2}) and Z=(x3,x4)Z=(x_{3},x_{4}). Then

H4=(A000).H_{4}=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}.

[detHess⁡(f)]6=detA⋅detHessZ⁡(f3).[\det\operatorname{Hess}(f)]_{6}=\det A\cdot\det\operatorname{Hess}_{Z}(f_{3}).
Proof.

A degree-six determinant term has entry degrees 2+2+1+12+2+1+1 or 2+2+2+02+2+2+0. A nonzero permutation term cannot contain three H4H_{4}-entries, because H4H_{4} is supported on only the two XX-rows and columns. With two H4H_{4}-entries, those entries exhaust both XX-rows and columns, leaving exactly the Z×ZZ\times Z minor of H3H_{3}. Summing the two block minors gives the displayed product with positive sign. ∎

Since the determinant is constant and the polynomial ring is a domain,

detHessZ⁡(f3)=0.\det\operatorname{Hess}_{Z}(f_{3})=0.

Write

HessZ⁡(f3)=(αββδ),\operatorname{Hess}_{Z}(f_{3})=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \beta&\delta\end{pmatrix},

where α,β,δ\alpha,\beta,\delta are linear forms and α​δ=β2\alpha\delta=\beta^{2}. HessZ⁡(f3)=λ​r​r𝖳.\operatorname{Hess}_{Z}(f_{3})=\lambda rr^{\mathsf{T}}.

The top remains independent of that coordinate, and f3f_{3} is affine-linear in it. Since f2f_{2} is quadratic, the whole polynomial has the form

f=P⁡(x1,x2,x3)+x4​Q​(x1,x2,x3)+a​x42,deg⁡Q≤2.f=P(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+x_{4}Q(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+ax_{4}^{2},\qquad\deg Q\leq 2. (2)

Proposition 5.3 (Degenerate structural reduction).

Both the genuinely binary and unary quartic cone tops reduce, after a constant linear change, to (2).

6 The uniform inversion proposition

Proposition 6.1 (Uniform inversion).

Let

f=P⁡(x1,x2,x3)+u​Q​(x1,x2,x3)+a​u2,deg⁡Q≤2,f=P(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+uQ(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+au^{2},\qquad\deg Q\leq 2,

where PP is arbitrary. If detHess⁡(f)=c∈ℂ×\det\operatorname{Hess}(f)=c\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}, then ∇f\nabla f is a polynomial automorphism.

Proof.

Write x=(x1,x2,x3)𝖳x=(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})^{\mathsf{T}} and set

M=Hessx⁡(Q),ℓ=∇Q​(0),v=∇Q=M​x+ℓ,B=Hessx⁡(P)+u​M.M=\operatorname{Hess}_{x}(Q),\qquad\ell=\nabla Q(0),\qquad v=\nabla Q=Mx+\ell,\qquad B=\operatorname{Hess}_{x}(P)+uM.

Then

Hess⁡(f)=(Bvv𝖳2​a).\operatorname{Hess}(f)=\begin{pmatrix}B&v\\ v^{\mathsf{T}}&2a\end{pmatrix}. (3)

7 Proof of the main theorem

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

By Lemma 2.1, detHess⁡(f4)=0\det\operatorname{Hess}(f_{4})=0. Theorem 2.2 reduces f4f_{4} to at most three variables. The classification of Section 3 is exhaustive.

If the cone top is genuinely ternary, Proposition 4.1 gives the common structural form. If it is genuinely binary or unary, Proposition 5.3 gives the same form. Proposition 6.1 then proves that ∇f\nabla f is a polynomial automorphism in every case. ∎

Corollary 7.1 (Quartic HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4}).

The Hessian conjecture in dimension four holds for every potential of degree at most four.

Proof.

Degrees at most two are affine-gradient cases, degree three follows from Wang’s quadratic Keller-map theorem, and degree four is Theorem 1.2. ∎

8 Discussion

8.1 What remains open

Theorem 1.2 proves the complete quartic case, not the full four-dimensional Hessian conjecture. For degree at least five, the top form is still a cone by Theorem 2.2, but the determinant contains more homogeneous layers and the degree-seven/six and degree-six/five arguments above do not carry over verbatim.

Proposition 6.1, however, has no degree bound on PP. Consequently it already proves arbitrary-degree cases which admit a coordinate form

P⁡(x1,x2,x3)+x4​Q​(x1,x2,x3)+a​x42,deg⁡Q≤2.P(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+x_{4}Q(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+ax_{4}^{2},\qquad\deg Q\leq 2.

8.2 Relation to the plane Jacobian conjecture

For a Keller map F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}, the potential

Φ⁡(x,y)=y𝖳​F​(x)\Phi(x,y)=y^{\mathsf{T}}F(x)

satisfies

detHess⁡(Φ)=(−1)n​(detJ​F)2,∇Φ​(x,y)=(J​F​(x)𝖳​y,F⁡(x)).\det\operatorname{Hess}(\Phi)=(-1)^{n}(\det JF)^{2},\qquad\nabla\Phi(x,y)=\bigl(JF(x)^{\mathsf{T}}y,F(x)\bigr).

Thus HC2​n\mathrm{HC}_{2n} implies JCn\mathrm{JC}_{n}. In particular, the full HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4} would imply the still-open JC2\mathrm{JC}_{2}, but the quartic result here addresses only a bounded-degree part of HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4}.
